map.theme: A terraced river valley at dawn, where a stream of softly glowing data droplets flows past paddy terraces, a busy market gate, a riverside repair workshop, a signal tower on a ridge and a hilltop observatory. The palette is misty teal, warm saffron and slate grey, and the mood moves from calm and curious in the valley to wide and confident at the summit.

scenarios.title: Forecasting Wheat Yield for Annadata Agri
scenarios.background: Annadata Agri Insights is a small agritech startup that advises farmer cooperatives in the fictional, canal-irrigated Vindhara district. It has 1,200 field records from three wheat seasons, each with rainfall, soil nitrogen, sowing date, fertiliser used and the final yield in quintals per acre; some records are missing the soil nitrogen reading. The cooperatives want a model that predicts each field's yield before harvest so they can book storage and transport in advance. Average yield across the records is about 14 quintals per acre.
constraints: Only 1,200 labelled field records are available
The team is two interns who are new to machine learning
Predictions must be honest estimates, because storage is booked from them

questions.prompt: The cooperatives want a predicted yield in quintals per acre for each field so they can book storage. Which kind of learning task should you set up?

options.text: Binary classification: high-yield vs low-yield field
Regression on yield in quintals per acre
Clustering fields into similar groups
Multi-class classification into yield bands such as 0-10, 10-20 and 20+

questions.explanation: The target is a continuous number, and the cooperatives need that number to size storage bookings. Regression predicts a continuous value directly, so it matches both the label and how the output will be used.

why_others_wrong.a: Two classes throw away the quantity the cooperatives need to book storage.
why_others_wrong.c: Clustering is unsupervised and ignores the yield labels you already have.
why_others_wrong.d: Bands give only a coarse range, so storage would still be over- or under-booked within each band.

questions.key_justification: A continuous numeric target that is used as a number calls for regression.

questions.prompt: A deep decision tree reaches a training RMSE of 0.4 quintals per acre but a validation RMSE of 3.1 quintals per acre. What does this gap most likely indicate?

options.text: The model is underfitting and needs more complexity
The validation records are probably mislabelled
The model is overfitting the training fields
The model just needs more training epochs to converge

questions.explanation: Near-perfect training error combined with much worse validation error is the classic sign of overfitting. The deep tree has learned noise specific to the training fields that does not carry over to new fields.

why_others_wrong.a: Underfitting shows high error on both training and validation, but training error here is very low.
why_others_wrong.b: Nothing points to bad labels, and a large train-validation gap is far more commonly explained by overfitting.
why_others_wrong.d: Decision trees are not trained in epochs, and training longer cannot fix a model that already fits the training data almost perfectly.

questions.key_justification: Low training error with high validation error means the model is overfitting.

questions.prompt: Which two changes are most likely to reduce this gap between training and validation error?

options.text: Increase the tree's maximum depth
Regularise the tree, for example by limiting depth or requiring more samples per leaf
Report training RMSE to the cooperatives, since it shows what the model learned
Collect more labelled field records
Retrain the same tree with a different random seed

questions.explanation: Regularisation limits how closely the tree can fit noise, and more data makes it harder to memorise individual records. Both directly attack overfitting.

why_others_wrong.a: A deeper tree has more capacity to memorise, which makes overfitting worse.
why_others_wrong.c: Training RMSE is over-optimistic and hides the real error on new fields, so it does not reduce the gap at all.
why_others_wrong.e: Changing the seed does not change the model's capacity, so the overfitting remains.

questions.key_justification: Overfitting is reduced by constraining model capacity or adding training data.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that gives an honest final estimate of how the model will perform on new fields.

options.text: Train candidate models on the training set
Evaluate the chosen model once on the held-out test set
Split the 1,200 records into training, validation and test sets
Fit the imputer for missing soil nitrogen on the training set only, then apply it to all three sets
Compare hyperparameter settings using the validation set

questions.explanation: Splitting first keeps the test set untouched, and fitting the imputer on training data only stops validation and test statistics leaking into the model. Tuning happens on validation, and the test set is used once at the end so its score stays unbiased.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Fitting the imputer on all 1,200 records before splitting, so the fill value is computed partly from test data, or tuning hyperparameters on the test set; both let test information leak in and inflate the final score.

questions.key_justification: The test set must stay untouched by preprocessing, training and tuning to give an unbiased estimate.

scenarios.title: Catching UPI Fraud at PaySetu
scenarios.background: PaySetu is a fictional UPI payments app processing about 2.4 million transactions a month. Roughly 0.2% of transactions are later confirmed as fraud. Each transaction has tabular features such as amount, hour of day, device age, whether the payee is new, and the number of transactions in the past hour. The fraud operations team wants a model that scores every transaction and flags suspicious ones for review.
constraints: Each transaction must be scored in under 50 ms
The fraud ops team can review only about 500 flagged transactions per day
Investigators want to see which factors drove each alert

questions.prompt: A teammate reports 99.8% accuracy for a model that never flags anything. Which evaluation should you use instead to compare fraud models?

options.text: Overall accuracy, measured on a much larger test set
Mean squared error of the predicted fraud probabilities
R-squared between the predicted and the actual labels
Precision and recall on the fraud class (PR curve)

questions.explanation: With 0.2% fraud, a model that predicts no fraud at all already scores 99.8% accuracy, so accuracy cannot separate useful models from useless ones. Precision and recall on the fraud class measure what matters: how many alerts are real and how much fraud is caught.

why_others_wrong.a: A larger test set does not fix the problem, because accuracy is dominated by the 99.8% legitimate transactions.
why_others_wrong.b: MSE on probabilities is also dominated by the majority class and does not show how well fraud is caught.
why_others_wrong.c: R-squared is a regression metric and is not meaningful for judging a rare binary class.

questions.key_justification: Under heavy class imbalance, accuracy is misleading and class-specific precision/recall is required.

questions.prompt: The ops team can investigate only about 500 flagged transactions per day, out of roughly 80,000. How should you set the alert threshold?

options.text: Flag the top ~500 scores a day and track their precision
Keep the default 0.5 threshold that most libraries apply
Flag every score above 0.01 so that recall is maximised
Choose the threshold that gives the best test-set accuracy

questions.explanation: The real constraint is review capacity, so the threshold should be set to produce about as many alerts as the team can handle. Precision among those top alerts then shows how much of the team's time is spent on real fraud.

why_others_wrong.b: 0.5 is an arbitrary default and, with rare fraud, may flag far fewer or far more than 500 transactions a day.
why_others_wrong.c: A very low threshold would produce thousands of alerts a day that the team cannot review.
why_others_wrong.d: Maximising accuracy pushes the threshold toward flagging almost nothing, because nearly every transaction is legitimate.

questions.key_justification: When review capacity is fixed, the threshold is set by alert volume and judged by precision at that volume.

questions.prompt: The features are tabular, scoring must take under 50 ms, and investigators want to see which factors drove each alert. Which model family is the best starting point?

options.text: k-nearest neighbours that searches all past transactions at scoring time
Linear regression on the 0/1 fraud label
Gradient-boosted decision trees on the engineered features
A large transformer trained from scratch on raw transaction logs

questions.explanation: Gradient-boosted trees are a standard strong baseline for tabular data, score quickly, and support per-prediction feature attributions for investigators. They meet all three constraints without needing massive data or hardware.

why_others_wrong.a: Searching millions of past transactions per request is slow and scales poorly against a 50 ms budget.
why_others_wrong.b: Linear regression is not designed for a binary label; its outputs are not bounded probabilities.
why_others_wrong.d: A large transformer from scratch needs far more data and compute, is hard to fit in 50 ms, and is harder to explain.

questions.key_justification: Gradient-boosted trees are the standard fast, explainable, strong choice for tabular classification.

questions.prompt: Which steps are sound ways to handle the 0.2% fraud rate during training?

options.text: Give fraud examples a higher class weight in the loss
Oversample fraud rows in the full dataset, then split into train and test
Oversample fraud rows within the training split only
Rebalance the test set to 50% fraud so the metrics look stable
Drop most fraud examples so the model is not confused by rare cases

questions.explanation: Class weights and training-only oversampling both make the model pay more attention to fraud without touching the evaluation data. The test set must keep the real 0.2% rate so that precision reflects what happens in production.

why_others_wrong.b: Oversampling before splitting puts copies of the same fraud rows in both train and test, which leaks data and inflates scores.
why_others_wrong.d: A 50% fraud test set makes precision look far better than it will be at the real 0.2% rate.
why_others_wrong.e: Removing fraud examples leaves the model even less signal about the class you need to catch.

questions.key_justification: Imbalance fixes belong in training only; the test set must keep the real class distribution.

scenarios.title: BazaarCart's Forecast Falls Apart
scenarios.background: BazaarCart is a fictional grocery chain with 140 stores. Its ML team trained a gradient-boosted model to forecast daily units sold per product per store, seven days ahead, using two years of history. Features include day of week, store floor area, sales 7, 28 and 365 days earlier, and a 7-day rolling average of sales. Offline, on a random 80/20 split of all rows, the model scored 6% MAPE, but after four weeks in production its MAPE is 31%. You find that the training notebook computed the rolling average using a centred window (three days before, the day itself and three days after), while the live service uses the previous seven days. The pipeline also fills any missing lag value with 0.
constraints: Replenishment orders are placed every evening from the forecasts
The fix must ship within one sprint
No new data sources can be added

questions.prompt: Which two practices in the original pipeline let future information into training or evaluation?

options.text: Using day of week as a feature
Computing the 7-day rolling average with a centred window
Using sales from the same week last year as a lag feature
Randomly splitting rows 80/20 across all dates
Using store floor area as a feature

questions.explanation: A centred window includes sales from days after the prediction date, which the live service can never know. A random split across dates lets the model train on later days and be tested on earlier ones, so it learns patterns from the future of its test rows.

why_others_wrong.a: The day of week is known in advance for any future date, so it leaks nothing.
why_others_wrong.c: Last year's sales for the same week are already known when the forecast is made.
why_others_wrong.e: Store floor area is a fixed attribute available at prediction time.

questions.key_justification: A feature or split is leaky when it uses information not available at the moment of prediction.

questions.prompt: After replacing the leaky feature, how should you split the data to estimate production performance honestly?

options.text: Train before a cutoff date, validate on the weeks after
Shuffled 5-fold cross-validation across all the rows
A random split of rows, stratified so every store appears
Hold out a random 20% of all products for validation

questions.explanation: In production the model always forecasts dates after the ones it was trained on. A time-based split reproduces that, so the validation score reflects real forecasting conditions.

why_others_wrong.b: Shuffling across dates still mixes future and past rows, recreating the same leakage.
why_others_wrong.c: Stratifying by store keeps every store balanced but still mixes dates randomly.
why_others_wrong.d: Holding out products tests performance on unseen products, not on future dates for known products.

questions.key_justification: Forecasting models must be validated on time periods after the training data.

questions.prompt: After the fixes, most regions show 14-16% MAPE, but 9 stores that opened three months ago show 40%. The pipeline fills missing lag values with 0. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The 7-day and 28-day lags are missing for these stores, so the model has no recent sales to learn from
MAPE is unreliable for stores with short histories, so the 40% figure is just a measurement artefact
New stores are a small share of the training rows, so the model needs more trees to fit them properly
The 365-day lag is missing for new stores, and the 0 fill tells the model they sold nothing last year

questions.explanation: Stores that opened three months ago have 7-day and 28-day history but no sales from a year earlier, so their 365-day lag is missing and gets filled with 0. The model reads 0 as a real value meaning very low demand, which pulls forecasts down for exactly these stores.

why_others_wrong.a: After three months of trading, sales from 7 and 28 days earlier exist for these stores, so those lags are not missing.
why_others_wrong.b: MAPE can be computed for any store with non-zero actual sales, and the 40% figure was already computed.
why_others_wrong.c: Adding trees does not change the false 0 input, so the model would still read these stores as having had no sales last year.

questions.key_justification: Filling missing values with 0 creates a false signal when 0 is also a meaningful real value.

questions.prompt: Match each symptom to the problem it most directly indicates.

items.text: Excellent offline score, poor production score; a feature used sales from days after the prediction date
Training and validation error are both high and close together
The same store-day gets different feature values in the training notebook and in the live service
Error was fine at launch and rises gradually after a new competitor changes local shopping habits

questions.explanation: Using future sales is leakage, and high error on both splits means the model is too simple to capture the pattern. Different feature values for the same row in two pipelines is training-serving skew, while gradual decline as the world changes is drift.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Matching i3 to target leakage: the problem there is that two code paths compute features differently, not that the features use future information.

questions.key_justification: Each failure mode has a distinct signature: leakage, underfitting, skew and drift.

scenarios.title: Routing Hinglish Tickets at VaaniCare
scenarios.background: VaaniCare is a fictional telecom operator whose support centre receives about 25,000 tickets a day from chat and transcribed calls, mostly in Hinglish. Tickets must be routed automatically into 12 intent queues such as billing, network issues, recharge failure and fraud or SIM-swap. The team has 18,000 tickets labelled with the correct intent. The fraud or SIM-swap intent is only 2% of tickets, but missing one is far more costly than misrouting a billing question.
constraints: Customer data must stay on the company's own servers
Only CPU servers are available, with no GPUs
Routing must take under 20 ms per ticket at the 95th percentile
The ML team has two people

questions.prompt: Given the constraints, what is the best first approach?

options.text: Send tickets to a hosted third-party LLM API and classify them zero-shot
Fine-tune a 7-billion-parameter language model and serve it on the CPU servers
Build a TF-IDF plus linear baseline, then test a small distilled transformer
Write keyword rules for each of the 12 intents, refined by the support team

questions.explanation: A TF-IDF linear model is fast on CPU, quick for a two-person team to build, and uses the 18,000 labels well, giving a strong baseline. Comparing a small distilled transformer against it shows whether extra accuracy is available within 20 ms.

why_others_wrong.a: Sending tickets to an outside API breaks the rule that customer data must stay on company servers.
why_others_wrong.b: A multi-billion-parameter model on CPU cannot classify a ticket in 20 ms.
why_others_wrong.d: Keyword rules are brittle with Hinglish spelling variation and ignore the 18,000 labelled examples.

questions.key_justification: Start with the simplest model that satisfies every hard constraint, then test heavier options against it.

questions.prompt: Customers write the same word many ways, for example 'nahi', 'nhi' and 'nahin'. Which text representation handles this best for the linear baseline?

options.text: Character n-gram TF-IDF features
Word-level TF-IDF with an English stop-word list
Bag of words using only the first five words of each ticket
Exact-match lookup against a standard Hindi dictionary

questions.explanation: Spelling variants share many character sequences, so character n-grams map them to overlapping features. Word-level features treat each spelling as an unrelated token.

why_others_wrong.b: Each spelling becomes a separate word token, and English stop words do not cover Hinglish.
why_others_wrong.c: Cutting to five words loses most of the content and does nothing about spelling variants.
why_others_wrong.d: Romanised Hinglish spellings rarely match standard dictionary entries exactly.

questions.key_justification: Character n-grams are robust to spelling variation because variants share substrings.

questions.prompt: The fraud or SIM-swap intent is 2% of tickets, and missing one is far costlier than misrouting a billing query. Which changes fit this situation?

options.text: Optimise overall accuracy only
Give the fraud intent a higher class weight during training
Use a lower decision threshold for the fraud intent than for other intents
Merge fraud into an 'Other' intent to simplify the model
Track recall for the fraud intent separately, alongside macro-F1

questions.explanation: Class weights and a lower threshold both push the model toward catching more fraud tickets, accepting some extra false alarms because a miss costs more. Tracking fraud recall separately makes sure that improvement is actually measured rather than hidden in an average.

why_others_wrong.a: Overall accuracy is dominated by the 98% non-fraud tickets and can stay high while most fraud is missed.
why_others_wrong.d: Merging fraud into 'Other' stops it reaching the fraud desk, which defeats the purpose.

questions.key_justification: Asymmetric error costs on a rare class call for weighting, a class-specific threshold and per-class recall.

questions.prompt: On held-out tickets, a small transformer scores macro-F1 0.86 at 45 ms p95 on CPU, and the linear model scores 0.81 at 4 ms p95. What should go live now?

options.text: The transformer, since its higher F1 matters more than latency
An ensemble that averages both models' predicted probabilities
The transformer on half the traffic, the linear model on the rest
The linear model, while the transformer is optimised for 20 ms

questions.explanation: The 20 ms limit is a hard constraint, and only the linear model meets it. Shipping it now and optimising the transformer separately keeps routing within budget without giving up the possible accuracy gain later.

why_others_wrong.a: At 45 ms the transformer breaks the hard 20 ms requirement, whatever its F1.
why_others_wrong.b: Averaging needs both models to run, so latency is at least the transformer's 45 ms.
why_others_wrong.c: Half the tickets would still exceed the 20 ms limit.

questions.key_justification: A hard latency constraint eliminates any option that cannot meet it, regardless of accuracy.

questions.prompt: Match each constraint to the design choice it makes unacceptable.

items.text: Customer data must never leave the company's own servers
Each ticket must be routed in under 20 ms (p95) on CPU-only servers
The fraud intent is only 2% of tickets

targets.text: Judging models by overall accuracy alone, which would hide missed fraud tickets
Uploading the 18,000 labelled tickets to an external cloud service to train the model offline
Running a multi-billion-parameter model on the company's own CPU servers for every live ticket

questions.explanation: Uploading tickets for offline training breaks only the data-residency rule; it adds no live latency and does not affect how models are compared. Running a huge model in-house keeps data on company servers but cannot meet 20 ms on CPU, and judging by overall accuracy alone fails only because fraud is so rare.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Matching the latency constraint to the external upload: training happens offline, so it adds nothing to per-ticket routing time and is ruled out only by the data rule.

questions.key_justification: Each hard constraint eliminates exactly one design choice: residency, latency or class imbalance.

scenarios.title: Credit Scoring for DhanSetu Microfinance
scenarios.background: DhanSetu Microfinance is a fictional lender giving loans of ₹20,000 to ₹1,50,000 to farmers and small shopkeepers across 60 districts. It wants a model that predicts, at the moment of application, whether a borrower will default, defined as becoming 90 or more days past due within 12 months. It has three years of history covering 210,000 loans, including application details, repayment records and collection activity. Model features include declared income, land holding, repayment history on earlier loans and a seasonal rainfall index for the borrower's district. The model will help loan officers decide approvals and will be retrained every quarter.
constraints: Every rejected applicant must receive specific reasons
Default labels take 12 months to mature
The model is retrained quarterly and must be monitored between retrains

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the right order for building and launching the default model.

options.text: Train and tune models on the earliest period, comparing them on the validation period
Define the label (90+ days past due within 12 months) and the prediction moment (the application date)
Deploy with monitoring of input drift, score distribution and early delinquency
Build features using only data available on or before each application date, and split loans by application date into training, validation and test periods
Calibrate scores, set the approval threshold with the credit team, then confirm once on the test period

questions.explanation: The label and prediction moment must be fixed first because they decide which data counts as a valid feature and how loans are split by time. Training, calibration and a single final test follow in that order, and monitoring begins only once the model is live.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Building features and splitting the data before defining the prediction moment, which makes it easy to include information that only exists after the application, such as collection activity.

questions.key_justification: The prediction moment defines what data is legal to use, so it must come before feature building and evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which candidate feature must be excluded from the model?

options.text: Land holding size declared at application
Monthly household income declared at application
Number of collection calls made to the borrower
Number of earlier loans repaid on time before this application

questions.explanation: Collection calls happen only after a loan is disbursed and usually after repayments start slipping, so they do not exist at the application date. Including them leaks the outcome into the features and makes offline scores look far better than live performance.

why_others_wrong.a: Land holding is declared at application, so it is available at prediction time.
why_others_wrong.b: Declared income is part of the application and is available at prediction time.
why_others_wrong.d: Earlier repayment history is known before the application and is a legitimate, useful feature.

questions.key_justification: Features must exist at the prediction moment; post-disbursal data is leakage.

questions.prompt: DhanSetu's policy requires a specific reason for each rejected applicant. Which approach meets this requirement?

options.text: Per-applicant reason codes from an interpretable model or attribution
The same global feature importance chart shown to every applicant
A note that the model decided, since it has been shown to be accurate
Publication of the training data so applicants can check it themselves

questions.explanation: The requirement is about each individual rejection, so the explanation has to be computed per applicant. Interpretable models or per-prediction attributions show which factors pushed that specific score toward rejection.

why_others_wrong.b: Global importance describes the model on average and does not say why a particular applicant was rejected.
why_others_wrong.c: Accuracy does not replace a reason, and this gives the applicant nothing specific.
why_others_wrong.d: Publishing borrower data is a serious privacy breach and still gives no reason for any single decision.

questions.key_justification: Individual reasons require per-prediction explanations, not global summaries.

questions.prompt: Seven months after launch, monsoon rains fail in 14 districts. Final 12-month default labels for recent loans will not exist for months. Which signals can warn you now?

options.text: Drift in input features such as declared income and rainfall index compared with training data
Training loss from the last quarterly retrain
Final 12-month default rate of loans issued last month
A shift in the distribution of predicted default scores
The early delinquency rate (30+ days past due) on recent loans

questions.explanation: Input drift and score distribution shift can be measured immediately on new applications, without waiting for outcomes. Early delinquency matures within weeks and acts as a leading indicator of the 12-month default label.

why_others_wrong.b: Training loss describes the data from the last retrain, not how the live population has changed since.
why_others_wrong.c: Loans issued last month cannot have a 12-month outcome yet, so this rate does not exist.

questions.key_justification: When labels are delayed, monitor inputs, score distributions and early proxy outcomes.

questions.prompt: Match each practice to the failure it guards against.

targets.text: A predicted 0.30 does not mean about 30% of such borrowers default
Evaluation looks better than reality because test loans come from the same period as training loans
Performance quietly degrades after launch as the borrower population changes
Features include facts that only exist after the loan was disbursed

questions.explanation: A time-based split stops evaluation from mixing periods, and point-in-time features stop post-application facts entering the model. Calibration makes scores usable as real probabilities, and drift monitoring catches decline after launch.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Swapping i1 and i2: both relate to time, but the split protects the evaluation, while point-in-time construction protects each individual feature value.

questions.key_justification: Each practice in the ML lifecycle protects against one distinct failure mode.
